newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Auckland economy slowing - Auckland City Council.
newsitem.headline: Auckland economy slowing - Auckland City Council.

text.p: The strong growth seen in the Auckland region over the past three years slowed during 1996, particularly in the third quarter, an Auckland City Council report published on Thursday shows.
The Auckland region comprises around a third of the country's economy, with an estimated annual GDP of NZ$29 billion.

The report shows a softening in the labour market. Auckland's labour force grew by 6.1 percent to 553,000 in the year to September and now constitutes 30.7 percent of the country's labour force. In the rest of New Zealand, labour force growth was moderate at 2.9 percent.
The council's report said the continuing labour force growth prevented any significant fall in unemployment in 1995. Unemployment rose 7.1 percent in the year to October 1996.
In line with the weaker labour market, average weekly wages rose only 0.2 percent in the August year, to NZ$659.
Annual job growth in the year to August was 5.5 percent.

The general economic hesitancy in the third quarter of 1996 translated itself into the Auckland housing market, but annually the strong growth in house prices continued. The average Auckland house price rose 16.4 percent to NZ$251,090 in the September year.
"The historically high level of recent housing development was maintained and the value of new houses built, at $1.26 billion, represented an increase of six percent," the council said.

Building activity remained strong across other sectors, with the vaue of industrial development in the Auckland region rising 91.7 percent to $227 million. Retail development rose 38 percent to $111 million, and office space development 26.5 percent to $135 million.
The council said analysts were divided over whether there would be strong movement again in the housing market in the summer months.
"Overall, house price growth should be at more modest, single digit levels," it said.
Retail sales were up 4.5 percent in the September year at $12.8 billion, compared to 3.7 percent growth in the previous year.
The council said while export growth had stalled as a result of the strong New Zealand dollar, the volume of imports through the Port of Auckland rose 15 percent in the September year.
"As New Zealand's import centre, a significant amount of Auckland's economic activity and jobs are in the sectors downstream associated with importing," it said.
Manufacturing exports were expected to pick up in the medium term when productivity rose as manufacturers adjusted to the strong currency.
"Growth in the finance and business services sector should continue to outstrip other sectors," the council said. However, any employment gains would be modest.

Immigration would continue to be an important factor in population and labour force growth in the medium term unless the new government curtailed it heavily, and unemployment was expected to rise again in 1997, the report said.
